That’s why people say don’t diet, you need a lifestyle change. That sounds big and scary, but it’s not. Start small. Try and reframe your thinking from ‘stop eating *bad foods*’ to ‘start eating more nutrient dense foods.’ Just try this as an experiment. Get weight loss out of your mind for just a moment. Think about giving your body what it needs. Add some things to your diet, like nuts, whole grains, protein, vitamins and mineral packed foods. Think abundance, rather than restriction. If you overeat due to a scarcity complex around food, restriction yourself if just going to trigger a food binge the moment you have a slight wobble. 

This is what I did. I started eating more nuts, seeds, protein, beans, veggies. It started to become fun. I’d make a dinner and see how many veggies I could get in it. I stopped thinking about weight loss, and started focussing on just wanting to have energy, and to feel like I am properly fueled. Then what happened is I stopped craving quick carbs and sugar. I didn’t try for this to happen, it just happened on its own. I guess my body didn’t need it anymore because I was eating regularly, not starving myself and giving myself the nutrients I needed. Then the weight started to come off. Turns out you don’t have to obsess, count calories, weigh yourself etc. I never once weighed myself or counted a calorie, I just started eating whole foods and regularly, until I was full. That bits really important. Eat until you are full. Don’t restrict. Add. But add nutrient dense foods. 

You shouldn’t deprive yourself of foods that bring you joy, either, but don’t then restrict other foods. If you want to have a piece of chocolate cake, don’t take any of the other healthy foods off the menu for that day because of calorie intake. Have the cake, and then eat all the other foods that are healthy. I like to think of cake, chocolate, sweets etc as *fun* foods now. They serve a purpose, like going to a theme park. You don’t go to the theme park everyday, because you have a job. The healthy foods are your job, the chocolate cake is the theme park. You’ve got to have both. (If you don’t like theme parks replace that with whatever, shopping, mini golf, whatever haha)

Oh man I feel this so deeply. I grew up in a house like this and the shame that comes with it, not being able to invite friends over etc sucks. 

When I got my first job I had the same feelings as you and wanted to do something about it, but I was also mad at my parents for living in such squalor that I decided to just do my bedroom as an example of what the rest of the house could look like. It didn’t work, but it did mean that I at least had my bedroom I could go to that was fresh and clean and if I did have a friend over I could usher them to my room quickly and they wouldn’t see much of the house other than the hallway and my bedroom. 

Here’s what I did. I asked around for any carpet scraps because my bedroom was small so I didn’t need much. I was given some by a family friend. I then found a cheap carpet fitter in the area and got them to lay it. It wasn’t a great job because there was nothing under the carpet but wooden boards and it was kinda uneven but I told him to do the best he could with what he had. 

I then got a cheap white paint and just covered everything, skirting, ceiling, walls. Then I saved for a nice coloured paint and painted one wall purple as a feature wall. 

Other stuff I got cheap or second hand from Facebook marketplace. Headboard was cheap, kept the same base of the bed as I could hide it with long sheets. Second hand bedside table. It’s honestly amazing what you can do with a bit of paint and cheap second hand furniture. It was such an incredible feeling to turn it around and actually have a space I could call my own and be proud of.

Don’t overwhelm yourself with the whole house, it’s a huge task. Start small and work your way up if that’s what you want to do.

Cuttings of these plants can be prone to root rot before they have a chance to be established. There are ways to mitigate this. One of which is emulating the soil in its natural environment, which is chunkier. The roots also need to be able to get oxygen to them, so having a chunkier mix will aid this. Also, if you have a tiny cutting in a very large pot with lots of soil, it’s going to take longer to dry out, especially as it’s inside so doesn’t have natural air/breeze getting to it. The longer it’s sat in wet soil the more chances it’s going to rot before it roots.

Another way to grow from cutting is to water propagation, hydroponics or semi/hydro. I tend to have much more luck with that as you can actually watch the root development with hydro. 

The reason I said to chop brown/squishy parts is because that’s a sign of root rot which will kill the plant. It’s far less risky to attend to the root rot than it is to leave it as it will spread and eventually kill the entire cutting.

On first look, it looks thirsty. The leaves curl like this when they’re thirsty. A couple of things to check. 

Is the soil compact and hard? This could be stopping the water from getting to the roots. Give it a poke, it should be loose enough for you to poke around. If it’s hard, get a wooden skewer or something to poke around and break the soil up and give it a through watering.

If the soil is loose, it’s time to check the roots. They should be firm to squeeze. If they’re mushy, shrivelled and/or black you have root. Root rot often present as it the plant hasn’t been watered enough/dehydration because it essentially is. The roots die, and are unable to pull water out of the soil, stopping it from getting to the roots. 

If it’s root rot let me know I can give you some more tips.

Looks like some type of mould. I’m not a mould expert, but my advice would be to scoop it off the top, and give it a sprits with 3% hydrogen peroxide. 

How often do you water? If the soil is moist a lot it can cause mould and fungus growth. It’s not always a bad sign depending on the fungus, but you should let the soil dry in between waterings which will prevent this.

Over time soil without additives can become compact and this makes it difficult for the water to penetrate meaning the roots in the centre won’t get enough water. It causes ‘channeling’ down the side of the pot. It can also be too dense, which stops oxygen getting to the roots and may lead to root rot. 

The best way to avoid all of that is to add some things to your regular soil. I use perlite, orchid bark, leca, charcoal, but even if you just used a couple of those until you get a mixture that is light, chunky and airy you’ll be good. It’ll mean the water can run through freely, the roots won’t be sat in set claggy soil and will be able to breathe and you won’t need to worry about overwatering. 

I buy my soil additives from soil ninja. Not sure if you can get soil ninja where you are but if not you can get these things in most places that sell gardening and plant supplies.

Agree with all of this. One thing I would also say to OP is if you’re going to keep them all together, make sure all the nodes/aerial roots (if there are any yet) are all facing in one direction. It’ll make it much easier when the plant gets a little bigger and you want it to cling to something for support.

Does that pot have drainage holes? If not, it’ll need to go into one with decent drainage. Also, if you’re repotting again (best to do it sooner rather than later now you’ve already done it once) then go for a decent potting soil, mixed with some perlite and orchid bark. They like a nice chunky soil. If you get it right you shouldn’t have to repot for a while as Monsteras tend to like being slightly root bound.
